venues.d: The city's grande dame — Art Deco poise that has anchored Mayfair for over a century.
Discreet, clubby and quietly grand — the address for those who prefer to be known, not seen.
Thames-side theatre and history — the London hotel everyone has heard of, and it earns the name.
The newest of the great houses — a Belgravia debut with the group's famous precision.
The Old War Office reborn — Whitehall grandeur turned into a hotel of real gravity.
Park-facing and precise — the group's London flagship, steps from Harrods.
Park Lane gold-leaf glamour — unapologetically grand, endlessly familiar.
A rooftop pool over the rooftops of Knightsbridge, and a fashion-literate wit throughout.
Regency splendour and a butler on every floor — old-world London at full volume.
Italian-jeweller cool below Hyde Park — the quiet, contemporary counterpoint to the grand dames.

venues.n: Four Seasons Hotel London at Park Lane
venues.d: The surest hands on Park Lane — service you never have to think about.
The Dorchester's chic younger sibling — Art Deco lines and Hyde Park at the window.
London's first all-suite hotel — the Maybourne group's most private new address.
Louis XVI gilt and the most famous tea in the world — Edwardian London, immaculately kept.
A vast, light-filled Victorian house between the river and Trafalgar Square.
A Belle Époque courtyard house that feels like a private London residence.
The original grand hotel of Europe — reborn, and still setting the standard for afternoon tea.
A landmark of old Regent Street, now a polished, design-led base at the heart of the West End.

venues.n: Brown's Hotel, a Rocco Forte Hotel
venues.d: London's oldest hotel — a warm, literary Mayfair townhouse of a place.
An Art Deco jewel with the ease of a private club — small, and all the better for it.
A Chelsea townhouse hotel with its own private garden square — rare, green and calm.
A members'-club-and-hotel in a Grosvenor Square mansion — the address of the moment.
The group's newer Mayfair house — contemporary calm off Hanover Square.
The old US Embassy on Grosvenor Square, reimagined as a grand all-suite house.
The last great family-owned London hotel — and the Royal Family's own choice.
A tucked-away St James's address with a famous American Bar and cobbled mews calm.

venues.n: Four Seasons Hotel London at Ten Trinity Square
venues.d: A Beaux-Arts landmark by the Tower — grand City grandeur with Four Seasons ease.
A sleek, tall City house with one of the best hotel pools in London.
A former bank turned all-day theatre — nine restaurants under a soaring banking hall.
A landmark Victorian palace on Russell Square — grand bones at a gentler price.
A contemporary Edwardian house with a chlorine-free pool, in the thick of theatreland.
The old police headquarters, now a characterful hotel a whistle from Trafalgar Square.
A row of Georgian townhouses in the heart of Mayfair — polished and well-placed.
A smart, contemporary base on Marylebone's village-like high street.
An eccentric, cocktail-loving townhouse with real personality.
A joyful, maximalist Soho debut — colour, a rooftop bar and a sense of fun.

venues.n: The Portrait by the National Portrait Gallery
venues.d: A small hotel atop the National Portrait Gallery, with a rooftop over Trafalgar Square.
Firmdale's English-country-house charm dropped into the middle of theatreland.
A hidden Soho urban village — bowling alley, roof garden and Firmdale colour.
A John Nash landmark with an indoor pool and Firmdale's fearless colour.
One of the city's handful of three-stars — Ducasse's grand French, immaculately kept.
The pink room everyone photographs — and cooking serious enough for three stars.
Clare Smyth's ode to British produce — the first UK woman to hold three stars.
Brett Graham's long-adored room, back at the very top after regaining its third star.
Ramsay's Royal Hospital Road flagship — the longest-held three stars in the country.
Darroze's warm, produce-led French, in one of Mayfair's most gracious rooms.
Classical haute cuisine in a gilded Louis XVI room — the UK's most celebrated dining room.
Claude Bosi's rooftop room at The Peninsula — refined French with a view.
London's most exciting kitchen — sub-Saharan flavours and spice, reimagined at the highest level.
The only two-star Chinese restaurant in Europe — regional China, exactingly rendered.
A wine-obsessed two-star from an ex-Fat Duck team — precise, and quietly brilliant.
Tom Sellers' narrative tasting menu — playful, personal, and technically superb.
A counter for a handful of guests, cooked right in front of you — intimate and exact.
A Brazilian-Italian tasting menu with real heart — one of the East End's finest tables.

venues.n: Alex Dilling at Hotel Café Royal
venues.d: Gossamer-fine haute French cooking above Regent Street — a serious two-star.
The colonial-club Indian room that raised the bar for the whole city — now two stars.
Anne-Sophie Pic's delicate, aromatic French, inside Ten Trinity Square.
Ex-Noma chef Santiago Lastra's Mexican — British ingredients, Mexican soul.
Tomos Parry's live-fire follow-up to Brat — Basque-leaning, and one of the hottest tables in town.
A long-running critical darling in Shoreditch Town Hall — modern British, quietly assured.
Coastal south-west Indian cooking in a stylish Marylebone room — the sister to Gymkhana.
Boundary-pushing Indian on Berkeley Square — a Mayfair fixture that changed perceptions.
London's oldest Indian restaurant, open since 1926 — and still holding its star.
The UK's first Punjabi restaurant to hold a star — a JKS ode to undivided Punjab.
Atul Kochhar's celebration of India's lesser-known regional kitchens.
Small Indian grill plates over open flame — light, sharing-led, and long-starred.
A rooftop sushi counter of great purity — Endo Kazutoshi's London omakase.
One of London's longest-standing starred rooms — refined French, quietly enduring.
A jewel-box Ginza-style omakase inside 45 Park Lane — the quietest luxury in Mayfair.
A tiny, revered sushi counter — one of the rarest seats in the city.
Angelo Sato's yakitori — every part of the bird over charcoal, and a star to show for it.
Heston's history-of-British-food, staged over Hyde Park at the Mandarin Oriental.
Marcus Wareing's polished, produce-led room in one of Knightsbridge's grand hotels.
The most wanted pub in London — a perfect pint, an open fire and Guinness done properly.
Adam Byatt's neighbourhood classic — the best table south of the river.
Full-flavoured French bistro cooking above a pub — critically adored, and good value for it.
Greek and eastern-Med cooking over fire in Borough Market — the highest new entry of its year.
Thai cooking through a British-seasonal lens — buzzy, personal and very hard to book.
Chet Sharma's inventive modern Indian — a Mayfair kitchen full of quiet ideas.
West African cooking from the first Black female chef to win a UK star.
Tomos Parry's original — whole turbot over fire, and a room that has never cooled.
A south-London institution — unshowy, French-leaning cooking of great consistency.
A West African tasting menu of real refinement — spice and craft in equal measure.
Vivek Singh's elegant Indian in the old Westminster Library — a grand, landmark room.
Mediterranean, live-fire cooking and warm personal service — SquareMeal's No. 1 London room.
The nose-to-tail temple that reshaped British cooking — plain, honest and iconic.
A fresh, modern take on South Indian — the chilli-cheese dosa has a following.
A Florentine trattoria run with love — simple, generous, and always full.
A tiny family-run Italian doing the cooking of Le Marche — the neighbourhood's pride.
Modern European cooking over live fire in a warm neighbourhood room.
Punchy, homestyle Malaysian cooking with a devoted local following.
Nigerian tapas in a joyful, generous room — sharing, done the West African way.
Honest, homestyle Korean cooking in an easygoing neighbourhood setting.
A small, wine-literate room doing precise modern-British plates.

Nine centuries of royal palace, fortress and prison on the Thames — come for the Crown Jewels, the Yeoman Warder (Beefeater) tour and the ravens. Book the first timed slot to beat the crowds around the jewels.
The coronation church of English and British monarchs since 1066, and burial place of kings, poets and scientists. The Poets' Corner and the high Gothic nave reward a slow, unhurried visit.

London's most-visited attraction and a free walk through world civilisations — the Rosetta Stone, Parthenon sculptures and the Egyptian galleries. Vast, so pick two or three galleries rather than trying to see it all; the Great Court is a fine place to regroup.
Wren's masterpiece with the second-largest cathedral dome in the world. Climb to the Whispering Gallery and on to the Golden Gallery for a City panorama, then find quiet in the crypt.

The monarch's official residence; the free Changing of the Guard ceremony (most days in summer, alternate days off-season) is pure London pageantry. In summer, the State Rooms open for tours — worth booking ahead for the throne room and picture gallery.

Free, and one of the great European painting collections — Van Gogh's Sunflowers, Turner, Vermeer, Caravaggio, all in one loop off Trafalgar Square. An hour with a handful of rooms beats a rushed march.

A former power station turned into the world's most-visited modern art gallery, with free collection displays and a top-floor viewing level over the river. Cross the Millennium Bridge from St Paul's for the classic approach.

The world's largest museum of art and design — fashion, jewellery, sculpture, Islamic and South Asian galleries under one roof, free to enter. The Jameel Gallery of Islamic art and the cast courts are highlights; the garden café is a lovely pause.

A cathedral-like Victorian building holding 80 million specimens — Hope the blue whale skeleton soars over Hintze Hall, and the dinosaur gallery is a guaranteed hit with children. Free, and multi-generation friendly.

The Palace of Westminster on the river, its Elizabeth Tower (Big Ben) freshly restored. UK and overseas visitors can tour the Commons and Lords, or simply photograph it from Westminster Bridge at dusk.

A UNESCO-listed botanic garden with over 50,000 living plants, the vast Victorian Palm House and Temperate House, and a treetop walkway. A green, restful full morning — easy and pram-friendly for a multi-generational group.

Stand astride the Prime Meridian at the Royal Observatory, see the Cutty Sark tea clipper and the painted hall of the Old Royal Naval College, with a skyline view back to the City. Arrive by river boat for the best of it.

London's oldest food market (trading since 1756) with 100-plus stalls of cheese, charcuterie, produce and street food. Go mid-morning on a weekday for room to graze; plenty of veg-friendly options among the stalls.

The observation decks of western Europe's tallest building, 244m up, with a near-360 sweep taking in Tower Bridge, the river and, on a clear day, out to the hills. Time it for sunset; private and premium ticket options exist.
A free, glass-domed public garden on top of the 'Walkie-Talkie' with 360-degree City views — book a timed slot in advance, or reserve a table at one of its restaurants for a guaranteed window seat.

London's most theatrical bridge; walk the high-level glass-floor walkway and see the Victorian steam engine rooms, or simply time a visit for a bascule lift (schedule published online). Best photographed from the South Bank.
Central London's great green lung — row or paddle on the Serpentine, walk to the Diana Memorial Fountain, or watch horses on Rotten Row. Speakers' Corner on a Sunday is a curiosity worth catching.

Formal rose gardens (12,000-plus blooms in Queen Mary's Garden), an open-air theatre in summer, and the climb up Primrose Hill for one of the city's finest protected skyline views. Bring a picnic for the hill at golden hour.

London's largest Royal Park — 2,500 acres of ancient oaks and free-roaming red and fallow deer, with the framed 'protected view' of St Paul's from King Henry's Mound. Feels like open countryside inside the city.

Wild, hilly heathland with the famous view from Parliament Hill, swimming ponds, and Kenwood House — a Robert Adam villa with free-entry old masters — at its northern edge. A proper lungful of countryside twenty minutes from the centre.

Pastel townhouses and the mile-long Portobello Road antiques market (best on Saturdays). Wander the quiet crescents and mews, browse the vintage and antique dealers, then find brunch on Westbourne Grove.

The restored market piazza with street performers under the glass roof, the Royal Opera House on the corner, and boutique-lined side streets. A natural base for a West End evening — theatre, dinner and people-watching.

One of the two great English-language theatre capitals — long-running musicals like The Lion King and Les Misérables alongside new plays and star-led runs. Book premium seats ahead; a matinee suits a family day.

Home of The Royal Opera and The Royal Ballet in a lavish Covent Garden theatre. See a performance, or take a daytime backstage tour and have a drink on the Paul Hamlyn Hall terrace overlooking the piazza.

London's most beloved recital hall, an intimate Arts-and-Crafts room celebrated for its acoustic and its chamber-music and song programme. For a connoisseur, an evening here is more rewarding than any big arena.
The legendary Soho jazz club, running since 1959, still the room where the great names play when in London. Book a table for the late set; small, dark and the real thing.

The best way to read the city — glide past Parliament, the Tate, Tower Bridge and Canary Wharf on an Uber Boat clipper down to Greenwich. A commentary sightseeing cruise or a private charter both work; UHNI groups can book a boat outright.
Painted narrowboats, willows and canalside cafés where two canals meet, with a towpath walk (or a canal boat) through Regent's Park and the zoo to Camden. A gentle, little-touristed slice of London.

The riverside promenade from Westminster past the London Eye, Southbank Centre, National Theatre and Tate Modern to Tower Bridge — street food, book stalls and skyline the whole way. The single best free walk in the city.

A free national museum in a Marylebone townhouse — Old Master paintings (Frans Hals' Laughing Cavalier), Sèvres porcelain, armour and gilt furniture, with a glass-roofed courtyard restaurant. An overlooked jewel a step off Oxford Street.

The house-museum of a great architect, left exactly as he arranged it — a labyrinth of antiquities, Hogarth's Rake's Progress and an Egyptian sarcophagus lit by hidden skylights. Free, small, and utterly singular; the candlelit evenings are magic.
A Victorian artist's fantasy home built around the Arab Hall — a domed courtyard glittering with antique Damascus tiles and a fountain. A jewel-box of a museum in leafy Holland Park.

A candlelit, immersive time capsule of a Georgian silk-weaver's house, experienced in silence as if the imaginary family has just left the room. Unlike anything else in London — book the atmospheric evening visit.

The royal grocer since 1707 — the food hall of hampers, teas and preserves is a destination in itself, and afternoon tea in the Diamond Jubilee Tea Salon upstairs is a classic. Excellent for gifts to take home.
The quintessential London ritual, served in the gilded Palm Court to a live pianist since 1906. Dress code applies (jacket and tie for gentlemen); a memorable occasion for a special family lunch.

The vast Knightsbridge department store — the food halls, the Egyptian escalator and every luxury house under one roof. Personal shopping and by-appointment services make it painless for serious buyers.

A mock-Tudor emporium built from old ships' timbers, famed for its printed fabrics, homeware and beauty hall — as much a piece of design history as a shop. The haberdashery and scarf rooms are a highlight.

The home of bespoke tailoring, where houses like Huntsman and Anderson & Sheppard have dressed the world for two centuries. Book a fitting for a made-to-measure suit — the London indulgence for the discerning gentleman.
A working royal residence set in Kensington Gardens, with the King's and Queen's State Apartments and rotating exhibitions of royal dress. Follow with tea at the Orangery in the gardens.

A single East End street erupting with cut flowers, plants and shrubs every Sunday, hemmed by independent shops and cafés. Go early for the colour and calm, later for the traders' end-of-day bargains.

East London at its most creative — street art, vintage stores, the Old Truman Brewery and one of the city's best concentrations of South Asian restaurants along Brick Lane. Sunday markets (UpMarket, Boiler House) are the day to come.

A sprawling warren of over 1,000 stalls by the canal — food from every corner of the world, vintage, music history and eccentricity. Loud and young; ride a canal boat in from Little Venice to arrive well.

Reborn Victorian coal warehouses turned into a design-led shopping and dining quarter beside the canal, next to Granary Square's fountains. Smart, calm and thoroughly contemporary — a good antidote to the tourist crush.

venues.n: Warner Bros. Studio Tour London – The Making of Harry Potter
venues.d: The actual sets, costumes and props from all eight films — the Great Hall, Diagon Alley and the Hogwarts model. A 20-mile trip north of the city; tickets are timed and must be booked well ahead. A sure-fire family day.

The oldest and largest occupied castle in the world and a favourite royal residence — the State Apartments, St George's Chapel and a Changing of the Guard of its own. Under an hour by train from Paddington or Waterloo.
The dreaming-spires university city — the Bodleian Library, Christ Church's great hall and quad, and a punt on the Cherwell. An hour by fast train from Paddington, walkable from the station.
A honey-stone Georgian city built around Roman baths and Jane Austen's world — the Roman Baths, the Royal Crescent and Bath Abbey, all on foot. About 90 minutes by train from Paddington.
The riverside university city — King's College Chapel, the colleges' hidden courts, and punting along the Backs past the great libraries. Under an hour by train from King's Cross.

Henry VIII's Tudor palace by the Thames — the great kitchens, the state apartments and the famous hedge maze in the formal gardens. Reachable by train from Waterloo, or grandly by river boat in summer.
The bar that redefined the hotel bar — twice the world's best, and still the finest martini in London, made at your table.
Two bars in one — a relaxed front room and a chef's-table counter where the ingredients change by the day.
A gentleman's-club snug of roaring fires, live jazz and Gerald Scarfe's caricatures, inside Rosewood London.
A cramped, cash-only East End room with taxidermy on the walls and some of the best drinks-making in the city.
A subterranean Mayfair den of Erik Lorincz's cocktail omakase — precise, personal, quietly world-class.

venues.n: A Bar with Shapes for a Name
venues.d: Remy Savage's Bauhaus-minded room — a menu built on ideas, in an East London bar that thinks like a gallery.
A tiny, brothers-run Soho bar doing classics with quiet modern precision — no theatre, just excellent drinks.

venues.n: The American Bar at The Savoy
venues.d: The oldest surviving cocktail bar in Britain — the birthplace of drinks the whole world now orders.
The Connaught's quieter salon — a fireside library of a bar, for conversation over a considered old-fashioned.
Black-and-gold Art Deco drama on the Savoy's old cabaret stage — theatrical drinks, live music.
Ryan Chetiyawardana's riverside laboratory — bold, ingredient-driven cocktails few other bars would attempt.
A quick aperitivo upstairs, a candlelit whisky den below — two moods, both faultless.
A 1920s speakeasy of live jazz and elaborate cocktails — London after dark at its most romantic.
The four-times World's Best bar at The Langham — a grand room that still makes ambitious, beautiful drinks.
Cocktails on the 31st floor of the tallest building in Western Europe — the whole city laid out beneath you.
London's longest rooftop bar — oysters, a spritz and an open sweep across the Thames to St Paul's.
A glamorous perch above the Strand with the river and the city's skyline in one glance.
